description:
## Contract risk

RFC 8620 §5.3 defines `ifInState` as a standard /set argument:

> if-in-state: 'String|null'  This is a state string as returned by the
> /get type request.  If supplied, the string must match the current state
> of the type, otherwise the method call will be rejected with a
> stateMismatch error.

This is the standard optimistic-concurrency primitive for JMAP /set
operations. Callers who race against other clients (or other workers in
their own backend) need it to detect and abort conflicting updates.

Canonical mail-client exposes the argument on `email_set`:

```rust
pub async fn email_set(
    &self,
    create: Option<serde_json::Value>,
    update: Option<HashMap<Id, PatchObject>>,
    destroy: Option<Vec<Id>>,
    if_in_state: Option<&State>,   // ← here
) -> ...
```

at crate-jmap-mail-client/src/methods/email.rs:104-109. The arg also appears
on `email_import` (line 253) and `email_submission_set`
(crate-jmap-mail-client/src/methods/submission.rs:165).

calendars-client `calendar_set`, `calendar_event_set`, and
`participant_identity_set` take NO `if_in_state` argument.

## Why this matters for a caller

Without `ifInState`, a caller cannot atomically guard a /set against
concurrent modification. They must implement defensive client-side state
tracking — retrieve the state from a prior /get or /set response, store it,
send the /set unguarded, parse the result, and if state has advanced
unexpectedly, refetch and replay. The server-side `stateMismatch` primitive
collapses all of that into a single round-trip.

This is exactly the use case for which the spec defined the argument. A
calendar-event editing app that wants to detect concurrent edits to the
same event (two users in the same shared calendar editing the same
recurring event) has no path through this client. Their fallback is to:

1. fetch the event's state via `/get` (one round-trip),
2. call `/set` with the patch (second round-trip),
3. parse the response state,
4. if drift detected, retry — but at this point the conflicting update has
   already been applied.

The canonical primitive replaces the four steps with one: pass the state
from step 1 as `ifInState` on the `/set` call, and the server atomically
either applies or rejects with `stateMismatch`.

## What goes wrong if this stays

A caller building a real multi-user calendar app on this client crate has no
correct path for concurrent-edit safety. They must either ignore the
problem (silent data loss in concurrent editing scenarios) or fork the
crate. Once shipped at 0.x.y, adding `if_in_state` is a breaking change
(new positional parameter, breaks all call sites).

The lack also creates an asymmetry: caller code that does
`sc.email_set(..., Some(&state))` for mail cannot do the equivalent for
calendar events. They have to know that calendar /set is fundamentally
non-atomic per the client they're using.

## Severity

Top priority among the supplement findings. This is a real callability
defect (the spec primitive is unreachable) AND a future breaking change to
fix.

## Fix shape

Add `if_in_state: Option<&State>` as the trailing positional argument to
all three `*_set` methods. Wire it into args as
`if let Some(s) = if_in_state { args["ifInState"] = s.as_ref().into(); }`
matching the canonical email.rs:115-117 pattern. Also extend
`event_notification.rs::calendar_event_notification_set` (destroy-only is
still spec-`/set` so the arg applies).

Workspace-wide implication: this is also a canonical-template propagation
candidate — if mail-client has it and calendars doesn't, contacts/tasks/
sharing/filenode siblings probably don't either. Worth surveying as a
follow-up sweep.
